content: Joanna Hoare, affiliated with the World Health Organization (WHO) in Switzerland, is one of the contributors to the WHO guidelines on mental health at work. Ehimare Iden, an Occupational Health and Safety Manager from Nigeria, has also contributed to this initiative. Hiroto Ito, from Tohoku Medical and Pharmaceutical University in Japan, and Norito Kawakami, from the University of Tokyo in Japan, have provided their expertise as well. Nour Kik, representing the Ministry of Public Health in Lebanon, and Enoch Li, from Bearapy in China, have also been involved in this work. Shuang Li, from the National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control at the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, has contributed to the guidelines. Sapna Mahajan, from Genome Canada, and Seyed Kazem Malakouti, from Iran University of Medical Sciences, have also played significant roles. Jason Maurer, from the WHO Regional Office for Europe, and María Elisa Ansoleaga Moreno, from Universidad Diego Portales in Chile, have provided their input. Kerri Nelson, from the Society for Human Resource Management in the United States, and Karina Nielsen, from the University of Sheffield in the United Kingdom, have contributed their expertise. Rory O’Neill, from the International Trade Union Confederation in Belgium, and Deirdre O’Shea, from the European Association of Work and Organizational Psychology in Ireland, have also been involved. Sudha P. Pandalai, from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and Cassie Redlich, from the WHO Regional Office for Europe, have contributed to the development of these guidelines. Claudia Sartor, from the Global Mental Health Peer Network in South Africa, and Khalid Saeed, from the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, have also been part of this effort. Dulani Samaranayake, from the University of Colombo in Sri Lanka, and Elena Shevkun, from the WHO Regional Office for Europe, have provided their expertise. Akihito Shimazu, from Keio University in Japan, and Ana Maria Tijerino Inestroza, from the WHO Regional Office for Europe, have also contributed. Victor Ugo, from the Mentally Aware Nigeria Initiative, and Ruth Wilkinson, from the Institution of Occupational Safety and Health in the United Kingdom, have been involved in this work. The WHO guidelines on mental health at work were developed with contributions from these experts and others. The guidelines aim to address mental health challenges in the workplace and provide evidence-based recommendations for creating supportive and safe working environments. The publication acknowledges the importance of mental health policies and practices in occupational settings and highlights the need for global collaboration to improve mental health outcomes for workers. The guidelines reference various resources, including the ILO-OSH 2001 guidelines on occupational safety and health management systems, and emphasize the importance of safe and healthy working environments free from violence and harassment. They also address the management of psychosocial risks in the workplace, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, and highlight the global burden of disease associated with long working hours and work-related stress. The publication includes data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Results Tool and the World Mental Health Report, which emphasize the need for transformative approaches to mental health. It also references studies on the economic costs of mental disorders and the return on investment in scaling up treatment for depression and anxiety. The guidelines underscore the importance of integrating health promotion into workplace occupational safety and health policies and provide practical recommendations for managing work-related psychosocial risks. The WHO and the International Labour Organization (ILO) jointly published these guidelines in 2022, with electronic and print versions available. The publication clarifies that the designations and material presented do not imply any legal status or endorsement of specific companies or products by WHO or ILO.
